claims.text: A model explicitly incorporating point defects, grain-boundary scattering, and oxygen impurities will predict bulk HfNbTaTiZr electrical conductivity more accurately than analytical models based on perfect crystals.
The proposed approach can integrate oxygen-induced defect sites and scattering centers into conductivity simulations.
The target material is conventionally processed bulk HfNbTaTiZr with controlled impurity content.
The target specimens include HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Defect-induced scattering may dominate electron mobility in HfNbTaTiZr at nearly 0–200 K.
Thermal excitations activate additional conduction channels in HfNbTaTiZr at 300–1200 K.
Defect dynamics become relevant to HfNbTaTiZr conductivity at 300–1200 K.
Vacancies, dislocations, and oxygen-associated sites alter electron mean free paths relative to an ideal HfNbTaTiZr crystal.
Defect scattering and defect- or oxygen-induced electronic-structure changes influence electron conduction in HfNbTaTiZr.
Low-temperature HfNbTaTiZr conductivity is governed by carrier freeze-out or defect-dominated scattering.
High-temperature HfNbTaTiZr conductivity involves thermally activated conduction and defect annealing or dynamics.
The proposed model will reduce conductivity prediction error from greater than 20% to below approximately 10% in both temperature regimes.
Conventional conductivity predictions for this alloy assume ideal, defect-free crystals and neglect microstructural defects and oxygen.
The model is applicable to bulk polycrystalline HfNbTaTiZr containing no more than approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The model's stated temperature domain is 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The model may be limited to specimens made under controlled processing conditions.
The quantitative error reduction and sensitivity to defect density and oxygen content remain uncertain pending experimental validation.
Failure to achieve a statistically significant error reduction from greater than 20% to below approximately 10% in either temperature regime would falsify the hypothesis.
